dharma_talks/S23E08_Apologies_I_tried_to.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth and a memorable personal framing (the Calcutta story, the dysentery monk) that pulls the listener toward compassion, and the practical catalogue of near-enemies and pitfalls is useful, but the self-admitted sprawl ('I've covered too much ground'), loosely sequenced concepts, and a meditation instruction that is brief and only lightly scaffolded prevent it from reaching the higher tier on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S23E09_2023_Oct_01_Good_Fri.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S23E09_2023_Oct_01_Good_Fri.title: 2023 Oct 01 'Good Friendship, Companionship, Good Comradeship is the Whole of the Spiritual Life.'
dharma_talks/S23E09_2023_Oct_01_Good_Fri.full_reason: A warm, personally authentic talk with a genuinely illuminating Ubuntu framing of kalyāṇamitta that earns its inspirational moments, but the meandering structure, the loose Satipaṭṭhāna exegesis (conflating the internal/external instruction with relational philosophy rather than staying precise about its meditative intent), and a few minor doctrinal imprecisions keep it from rising above solidly good.
dharma_talks/S23E09_2023_Oct_01_Good_Fri.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, a memorable Ubuntu framing, and an authentic personal voice that makes the teaching accessible and at times moving, but it meanders through loosely connected examples (proprioception, the feral child, lèse-majesté) without a clearly sequenced argument or actionable guidance, leaving the central insight about kalyanamitra only partially developed.

dharma_talks/S23E10_2021_Gratitude_Gener.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S23E10_2021_Gratitude_Gener.title: 2021 Gratitude, Generosity and Renunciation
dharma_talks/S23E10_2021_Gratitude_Gener.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's warm, anecdote-rich delivery makes the gratitude-generosity-renunciation trilogy genuinely engaging and practically actionable, though the talk stays at a fairly accessible rather than deeply penetrating level, and a few doctrinal edges are slightly soft (e.g., the near-equation of generous letting-go with a 'touch of nirvana' is evocative but imprecise, and the claim that the trilogy 'is not actually taught in the scriptures themselves' is asserted without nuance), keeping both scores solidly in the strong-but-not-outstanding range.
dharma_talks/S23E10_2021_Gratitude_Gener.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personal, and accessible talk with memorable anecdotes (the dentist, the painting favor, gift-giving ritual) and a genuinely useful framing of the gratitude-generosity-renunciation loop as lived daily practice, but the instruction remains largely attitudinal rather than step-by-step, the conceptual distinctions (especially around renunciation and attachment) are suggestive rather than precise, and the structure meanders enough to dilute both its inspirational force and its practical clarity.

dharma_talks/S23E11_2022_Jul_17_Need_Suf.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S23E11_2022_Jul_17_Need_Suf.title: 2022 Jul 17 Need, Sufficiency and Greed -
dharma_talks/S23E11_2022_Jul_17_Need_Suf.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's talk is warm, practical, and refreshingly grounded in lived monastic experience, with charming personal anecdotes and useful reflective exercises, but it stays largely at the level of pragmatic lifestyle advice rather than connecting sufficiency and non-greed deeply to the Dhamma (e.g., dependent origination, the role of taṇhā, the noble eightfold path), and the doctrinal content, while not seriously wrong, is thin and occasionally imprecise (e.g., the simplified treatment of the three robes, the somewhat uncritical medical endorsement of fermented cow's urine), leaving the talk solid but unremarkable on both dimensions.
dharma_talks/S23E11_2022_Jul_17_Need_Suf.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and some memorable anecdotes (the 12-degree practitioner, the childhood butter-scraping, the three robes story) that give it an accessible, conversational charm, but it meanders without a clear meditative or contemplative structure, the practical exercises are sketched rather than developed, and the framing around need/sufficiency/greed never coalesces into actionable guidance a practitioner could carry into formal practice or daily life with confidence.

dharma_talks/S23E12_2025_Apr_06_Renuncia.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S23E12_2025_Apr_06_Renuncia.title: 2025 Apr 06 Renunciation.
dharma_talks/S23E12_2025_Apr_06_Renuncia.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practically grounded, and doctrinally faithful treatment of renunciation—correctly rooting it in taṇhā, anattā, and sammā-saṅkappa, with vivid everyday examples—but the talk is more quietly wise than electrifying, and a few moments (the Zen 'no preference' citation, the boredom/disinterest distinction) are suggestive rather than rigorously unpacked, keeping both scores solidly strong without reaching the outstanding tier.
dharma_talks/S23E12_2025_Apr_06_Renuncia.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personally grounded, and wide-ranging talk with memorable framings (boredom vs. disinterest, the 'little demon lying low', the Zen 'no preference') and practical graduated guidance that genuinely motivates practice, held back slightly by loose structural sequencing, an abrupt pivot from formal Eightfold Path exposition to lifestyle applications, and meditation instructions that are gestured at rather than precisely developed.

dharma_talks/S23E13_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S23E13_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S23E13_Video.full_reason: A genuinely thoughtful and doctrinally careful exploration of hope, aspiration, and faith in Theravāda practice—anchored by solid Pali terminology (chanda, saṃvega, taṇhā, paṇidhāna), honest personal reflection, and the memorable process-over-progress conclusion—but the delivery is somewhat meandering and the treatment of Mahāyāna concepts, the consciousness-without-boundary gloss on Nibbāna, and the brief rebirth reassurances on the deathbed are underdeveloped or lightly handled, keeping it from outstanding on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S23E13_Video.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma brings genuine warmth, personal anecdote, and a well-chosen central distinction (aspiration vs. expectation) that is both memorable and practically motivating, but the talk's structural looseness—meandering through Pali terms, Mahāyāna detours, and the somewhat tangential death-and-rebirth section—dilutes both its inspirational arc and its instructional precision, leaving the meditator with a useful framing but imprecise guidance on how to actually apply it in practice.

dharma_talks/S24E01_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S24E01_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S24E01_Video.full_reason: A warm and accessible survey of the nine Buddhist qualities of the Buddha with some memorable analogies (Hillary/Tenzing, the internal realms), but the doctrinal treatment is uneven—conflating the six realms cosmology with purely psychological states without noting this is one interpretive lens, the etymology of 'arahant' is presented as settled when it is contested, and key terms like vipassanā are introduced but not substantively explained—leaving the talk pleasant and well-intentioned but lacking the depth and precision to score highly on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S24E01_Video.craft_reason: The talk offers warmth and accessible analogies (Hillary climbing Everest, the hungry-ghost realm as greed) and a clear organizational spine in the nine qualities, but it remains a fairly light survey — meditation instruction is minimal, the psychological reframings of the realms are suggestive but underdeveloped, and the devotional content never quite builds to genuine inspirational momentum.

dharma_talks/S24E02_The_Buddha_and_War.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S24E02_The_Buddha_and_War.title: The Buddha and War
dharma_talks/S24E02_The_Buddha_and_War.full_reason: The talk offers genuinely interesting historical vignettes and a thought-provoking pacifism/non-violence distinction, delivered with an authentic, unpretentious voice, but it remains loosely structured, the doctrinal analysis is thin and occasionally speculative (e.g., attributing motives to the Buddha without textual grounding, the Shaolin/samurai digression sits uneasily in a Theravāda frame), and it stops short of deepening the listener's understanding of kamma, intention, or cetanā with enough precision to be fully sound or truly inspiring.
dharma_talks/S24E02_The_Buddha_and_War.craft_reason: The talk offers a genuinely interesting ethical framing (pacifism vs. nonviolence, the kamma lens on war) and some evocative historical vignettes, but it meanders without a strong through-line, the samurai digression is underdeveloped, the concluding practical guidance is thin and hedged to the point of vagueness, and it contains no meditation instruction or actionable practice guidance to ground its insights.

dharma_talks/S24E03_2025_May_04_The_Budd.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S24E03_2025_May_04_The_Budd.title: 2025 May 04 The Buddha as a Teacher.
dharma_talks/S24E03_2025_May_04_The_Budd.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a doctrinally faithful and carefully structured presentation of the Cūḷamāluṅkya Sutta—accurate on the four noble truths, the Buddha's silence on metaphysics, and the anattā implication behind the undeclared questions—while the pedagogical meta-commentary is genuinely illuminating, though the talk remains more instructive than deeply moving, with modest narrative warmth and limited evocation of the lived urgency of practice.
dharma_talks/S24E03_2025_May_04_The_Budd.craft_reason: A warm, well-structured talk that skillfully unpacks the Buddha's pedagogical method through the Malunkyaputta sutta — clear, gently charming, and practically illustrative — but it stays largely expository rather than igniting the listener's own practice, and the meditation/practice dimension is thin enough to limit both inspirational impact and actionable guidance.

dharma_talks/S25E01_2025_June_08_What_wa.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S25E01_2025_June_08_What_wa.title: 2025 June 08 What was the Buddha's great disovery?
dharma_talks/S25E01_2025_June_08_What_wa.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely warm and intellectually engaging talk with memorable framings—the bubble of consciousness, the hotel-room awakening, Ajahn Mahābua's spontaneous insight—that authentically point toward Nibbāna's transcendence, while remaining doctrinally faithful to the Udāna passages and anattā teaching, though the discussion of 'unconditioned citta' risks implying a substantialist reading that edges toward the very ātman view the Buddha rejected, and the closing instruction to 'turn attention toward the three characteristics' is somewhat vague as practical guidance.
dharma_talks/S25E01_2025_June_08_What_wa.craft_reason: The talk carries genuine warmth, memorable framing (the house-builder metaphor, the hotel-room awakening moment), and an authentic contemplative voice that inspires curiosity about Nibbāna, but the craft is uneven—meditation instructions are largely absent or gestured at rather than sequenced, key terms (citta, āyatana, dimension) shift in usage without precise anchoring, and the closing pivot to 'turn attention toward the three characteristics' is too abrupt to be practically actionable, leaving the talk inspiring in spirit but insufficiently rigorous in craft to score high on both dimensions simultaneously.

dharma_talks/S25E02_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S25E02_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S25E02_Video.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's patient, scholarly unpacking of the Kevaṭṭha Sutta and the nature of Nibbāna is doctrinally careful and occasionally enlivened by dry wit (the satire on Brahma), but the talk remains largely expository rather than deeply moving, the 'luminous consciousness' passages risk blurring the line between nibbāna and the ālayavijñāna without sufficient caveat, and the ending is too brief to fully land the profound territory it opens.
dharma_talks/S25E02_Video.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine scholarly depth and an engaging narrative arc through the Kevaddha sutta, with moments of warmth and dry wit, but the doctrinal exposition of Nibbāna consciousness remains conceptually muddy and the practical bridge to actual meditation practice is thin and abrupt, leaving the listener intellectually stimulated but insufficiently equipped or moved to sit.

dharma_talks/S25E03_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S25E03_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S25E03_Video.full_reason: The talk is genuinely evocative—the Narcissus metaphor, the baby-development analogy, and the Mae Chi Kiao quote are memorable and warmly delivered—but doctrinal tensions arise in equating sati with a permanent 'unborn, undying' observer-self that is 'whole, entire and permanent,' which risks implying a subtle ātman view at odds with strict anattā teaching, and the claim that the perceiver 'cannot be arising and passing away' is presented as settled doctrine rather than a pointer requiring careful qualification.
dharma_talks/S25E03_Video.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely moving and conceptually rich talk — the Narcissus metaphor, the baby-development arc, and Mae Chi Kiao's closing testimony are memorable and warmly rendered — while the meditation instructions, though somewhat advanced and occasionally impressionistic ('gaze with wonder,' 'presume the awareness knows what it's looking for'), are coherent, sequenced, and practically followable, making this a strong if not outstanding offering on both dimensions.

dharma_talks/S26E01_2024_April24_Contemp.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E01_2024_April24_Contemp.title: 2024 April.24 Contemplating the Unpleasantness of the Body.
dharma_talks/S26E01_2024_April24_Contemp.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, humanly engaging talk with memorable framings (the realms as mental states, the apology to the body, the striking historical account of the monks' suicides) and technically faithful asubha instruction drawn directly from the Giramananda Sutta and Dhammapada, though the doctrinal framing of the realms is presented somewhat loosely, the added 'cancer' caveat is endearingly honest but slightly undermines authority, and the closing gratitude-to-the-body pivot, while pastorally skillful, sits in mild tension with the classical asubha purpose without that tension being fully resolved.
dharma_talks/S26E01_2024_April24_Contemp.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, a memorable dark-humor tone, and a striking cautionary story about the monks' suicides that creates real urgency, but the meditation instructions are loosely sequenced and underdeveloped — the 'catch your disgust and ask if it's necessary' guidance is too thin to be reliably actionable, and the pivot to gratitude practice, while charming, is introduced too abruptly to be well-integrated craft.

dharma_talks/S26E02_2024_June_23_The_Una.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E02_2024_June_23_The_Una.title: 2024 June 23 The Unattractive Nature of the Body
dharma_talks/S26E02_2024_June_23_The_Una.full_reason: The talk is warmly delivered and creatively structured—balancing asubha contemplation with a gratitude practice is a genuinely helpful pastoral move—and the turtle simile and the Vesālī suicide story are well used, but soundness is undermined by the loose framing of Māra (conflating Buddhist and Islamic concepts), the claim that 'the king of death' in the Dhammapada verse means 'spiritual death' rather than Māra/death itself, the somewhat cavalier glossing of the grave asubha-suicide episode without adequate safety guidance for modern practitioners, and minor doctrinal imprecision throughout, keeping the overall score in the solid-but-flawed range.
dharma_talks/S26E02_2024_June_23_The_Una.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, a memorable story (the monks' suicides), and a structurally appealing three-part arc (preciousness → repulsiveness → gratitude), but the meditation instructions are loosely sequenced and underdeveloped, the key transitions lack clear guidance for practitioners, and the conceptual framing (why disgust should resolve and how gratitude balances it) is asserted rather than explained, leaving both the inspirational and practical dimensions competent but unremarkable.

dharma_talks/S26E03_I_own_my_actions_I_i.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E03_I_own_my_actions_I_i.title: I own my actions. I inherit the results of my actions. I am born of my actions. I form relations through my actions. I live dependent on my actions. Whatever I do for good or for ill, I shall inherit the results.VideoKarma and Rebirth
dharma_talks/S26E03_I_own_my_actions_I_i.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personally honest, and practically grounded talk on kamma that is genuinely engaging—bolstered by the Hoddle anecdote, the Navalny reference, and the Ubuntu parallel—while remaining largely faithful to the Pali sources, though the doctrinally important but casually handled claim that 'the body you receive is not the direct consequence of your past actions' and the brief mention of using GPT slightly undercut both the depth and the authority expected of an outstanding dharma talk.
dharma_talks/S26E03_I_own_my_actions_I_i.craft_reason: The talk carries genuine warmth, intellectual honesty (including the charming GPT admission), and vivid illustrative moments—Navalny, the two disabled siblings, the Hoddle anecdote—that make karma feel lived-in rather than abstract, while the structured six-phrase contemplation framework is clear and practically followable, though the conceptual transitions are occasionally loose, the rebirth material is briefly asserted rather than unpacked, and the guided contemplation itself is somewhat sparse in bridging instruction between intellectual reception and experiential absorption.

dharma_talks/S26E04_Karma_and_Rebirth.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E04_Karma_and_Rebirth.title: Karma and Rebirth
dharma_talks/S26E04_Karma_and_Rebirth.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, accessible, and genuinely encouraging talk with some memorable framings (karma as individual moral responsibility, the 'five niyāmas' framework, the house-builder verse), but the doctrinal handling is uneven—the characterisation of the vipassanā observer as a place of 'untouchability' and 'the Buddha within' risks reifying a witnessing self in a way that sits uneasily with anattā, the treatment of mind-body dualism ('two separate energy systems') is not standard Theravāda Abhidhamma, and the five niyāmas are introduced but left partially explained—limiting its overall score despite solid ethical grounding and an encouraging pastoral tone.
dharma_talks/S26E04_Karma_and_Rebirth.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and some evocative moments (the house-builder verse, the 'untouchability' of the observer, the pragmatic handling of rebirth doubt) that give it modest inspirational lift, but the structure is loose and meandering, key concepts (citta as psychology vs. citta as knowing-awareness, the five niyāmas) are introduced inconsistently or left underdeveloped, and the meditation instruction is too thin and vague to be practically actionable, keeping both dimensions solidly in the middle range.

dharma_talks/S26E05_2023_Nov_26_The_Five.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E05_2023_Nov_26_The_Five.title: 2023 Nov 26 The Five Regular Contemplations.

dharma_talks/S26E05_2023_Nov_26_The_Five.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personable, and occasionally witty exploration of the five contemplations with genuinely useful practical instructions (the heart-surrender method, phrase repetition, the two lists exercise), but both dimensions are held back by loose structuring, an abrupt treatment of kamma, and meditation guidance that, while evocative, lacks the precision and sequencing needed to fully anchor a practitioner's independent practice.

dharma_talks/S26E06_2022_Nov_06_The_Cont.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E06_2022_Nov_06_The_Cont.title: 2022 Nov 06 The Contemplation of Death.
dharma_talks/S26E06_2022_Nov_06_The_Cont.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely moving and doctrinally well-grounded talk on maraṇasati—anchored in canonical phrases, Ernest Becker's resonant framing, and vivid images (the toast, the Zen monk, the memento mori)—with the contemplative phrases closely tracking the AN sutta on death-mindfulness and the kamma reflection drawn accurately from the Upajjhatthana Sutta, though the overall score is tempered slightly by the talk's somewhat loosely structured middle section and the Catholic purgatory analogy, which, while charming and pedagogically useful, blurs doctrinal lines without explicit disambiguation.
dharma_talks/S26E06_2022_Nov_06_The_Cont.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warmly personal, genuinely moving talk with memorable images (the toast-and-marmalade heart attack, the Zen monk admiring a wildflower while hanging from a cliff) and a clear practical structure—three progressive contemplative phrases for sickness, aging, and death—but the meditation instructions, while usable, are lightly scaffolded (minimal guidance on what to do with arising resistance beyond 'wait for it to die') and the talk's structure meanders enough between autobiography, doctrine, and practice that a new practitioner might struggle to extract a clean, sequenced method.

dharma_talks/S26E07_The_Eight_Worldly_Wi.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S26E07_The_Eight_Worldly_Wi.title: The Eight Worldly Winds
dharma_talks/S26E07_The_Eight_Worldly_Wi.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, grounded, and doctrinally faithful exploration of the eight worldly winds—rooted in accurate sutta references, sound psychological observation, and practical reflective exercises—but the talk's inspirational force is somewhat diluted by its discursive, meandering structure, and a brief passage on assisted dying, while pastorally sensitive, ventures into ethically contested territory without the careful nuance the topic demands, slightly compromising both the conceptual rigor and the overall lift of the teaching.
dharma_talks/S26E07_The_Eight_Worldly_Wi.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practically grounded and occasionally vivid talk — the 'one less lunch' image, the fantasies of revenge, the cake and hunger distinction all land well — but the discourse meanders through its eight topics without tight structure, the digression into assisted dying feels unintegrated, and the meditation instructions (bring a past event to mind, feel the craving, name it) are suggestive rather than precise, leaving the talk solidly useful and genuinely human but short of outstanding on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S27E01_The_Paradox_of_Fear.title: The Paradox of Fear
dharma_talks/S27E01_The_Paradox_of_Fear.full_reason: A warm, doctrinally grounded talk drawing on the Bhayabherava Sutta and Dhammapada with genuine practitioner authenticity and useful mettā/vipassanā framing, though the inspirational arc is somewhat rambling and the meditation guidance on 'holding fear with care' could be more precisely situated within formal practice instructions.
dharma_talks/S27E01_The_Paradox_of_Fear.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma brings genuine warmth, self-deprecating humor, and a well-chosen sutta reading that grounds the talk, but the instruction on working with fear (the 'holding with care' method) is underdeveloped and the overall structure meanders between phenomenology, practice guidance, and conceptual analysis without fully resolving into a clear, actionable sequence a practitioner can confidently follow.

dharma_talks/S27E02_2025_Jan_12_Dukkha_-.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E02_2025_Jan_12_Dukkha_-.title: 2025 Jan 12 Dukkha - the Buddha grounds his teaching on this word

dharma_talks/S27E02_2025_Jan_12_Dukkha_-.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, etymological richness, and a clear map of dukkha's three forms and Four Noble Truths, but the digression into political ideologies (neoliberalism, communism, nazism) dilutes focus and the meditation-practice implications remain somewhat underdeveloped, leaving both inspiration and practical craft solid but not outstanding.

dharma_talks/S27E03_2024_Feb_25_The_cruc.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E03_2024_Feb_25_The_cruc.title: 2024 Feb. 25 The crucial role of Desire and Intention.

dharma_talks/S27E03_2024_Feb_25_The_cruc.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, well-structured, and practically grounded talk with memorable illustrations (stone-throwing, pot-washing, sticky toffee pudding, the mobile phone theft sequence) and genuine humor that sustains engagement, while the conceptual distinctions between taṇhā, chanda, and cetanā are drawn clearly and sequenced logically—though the talk is more expository than deeply moving, the practical anchoring to daily-life intention-watching is solid and actionable, leaving only minor weaknesses in transitional clarity and depth of inspirational uplift.

dharma_talks/S27E04_2024_July_14_The_Fou.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E04_2024_July_14_The_Fou.title: 2024 July 14 The Four Great Elements

dharma_talks/S27E04_2024_July_14_The_Fou.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a warm, learned, and practically grounded talk with genuinely useful deconstruction exercises and memorable framings (pain as mental construct, 'plunging into the object'), but the inspiration is modestly capped by a discursive, somewhat meandering structure and a closing that trails off rather than building to a memorable summit, while the soundness is solid though the guided exercise is loosely sequenced and the explanatory connections between doctrine and practice are occasionally left implicit rather than made crisp.

dharma_talks/S27E05_2024_August_18_The_S.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E05_2024_August_18_The_S.title: 2024 August 18 The Specific Law of Conditionality

dharma_talks/S27E05_2024_August_18_The_S.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine intellectual warmth, vivid real-world examples (Greta Thunberg, Archduke Ferdinand, the reformed politician), and an authentic conversational voice that keeps the listener engaged, but it meanders across philosophy, social commentary, and kamma without a tight throughline, and its meditation/practice instructions are almost entirely absent, leaving a practitioner with interesting ideas but little concrete guidance on how to actually work with conditionality in sitting or daily practice.

dharma_talks/S27E06_2024_September_15_Th.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E06_2024_September_15_Th.title: 2024 September 15 The Dangers of Indulgence
dharma_talks/S27E06_2024_September_15_Th.full_reason: The talk is warm, practical, and gently compelling—with memorable images like the Christmas cake metaphor, the Greek myth, and the 'blank TV screen' exercise—while remaining doctrinally sound in its framing of the middle path, tanhā, and renunciation, though it occasionally slides into imprecision (conflating Māra's daughters with 'boredom,' a loose rendering of the simile; the claim that Nibbāna equals 'contentment and happiness' is only partially accurate and could mislead) and the practical renunciation instructions, while sensible, are sketched rather than fully developed.
dharma_talks/S27E06_2024_September_15_Th.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, memorable images (the Christmas cake marzipan, Erysichthon, the empty cup exercise), and a practically useful five-part taxonomy of indulgence's aftermath, but the structure meanders without tight sequencing, the three stated distinctions (enjoyment vs. indulgence, body vs. mind, desire vs. action) are announced then largely dropped in favour of free association, and the meditation instruction—while charming—is brief and underdeveloped, leaving the talk more as a reflective essay than actionable practice guidance.

dharma_talks/S27E07_2023_Jan_08_The_Four.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E07_2023_Jan_08_The_Four.title: 2023 Jan. 08 The Four Bases of Power :
dharma_talks/S27E07_2023_Jan_08_The_Four.full_reason: The talk is warm and accessible with a relatable personal anecdote, but it is doctrinally thin—omitting viriya as a distinct base and conflating citta with what the Pāli sources distinguish as a fourth factor (vīmaṃsā explained imprecisely), while the treatment of iddhis and the overall framing remains too cursory to be either deeply inspiring or technically rigorous.
dharma_talks/S27E07_2023_Jan_08_The_Four.craft_reason: The talk is warm and accessible, with a charming personal anecdote and genuine encouragement, but it remains surface-level on both dimensions — the four bases are introduced rather than deeply explored or practically sequenced for meditation use, and while the voice is likeable, the content lacks the memorable imagery, emotional depth, or actionable precision needed to genuinely move practitioners or provide rigorous, followable instruction.

dharma_talks/S27E08_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E08_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S27E08_Video.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practically grounded, and genuinely moving exposition of the spiral path (paṭicca-samuppāda's liberative sequence), weaving climate anxiety into the teaching with memorable concreteness and helpful calibration of expectations, while remaining doctrinally faithful; minor deductions arise from the slightly imprecise characterisation of vipassanā as 'simply observe, don't interfere' and the presentation of the spiral stages (rapture, tranquility, happiness, samādhi) in a way that occasionally blurs canonical pīti/passaddhi/sukha/samādhi distinctions, but these are modest blemishes in an otherwise sound and inspiring talk.
dharma_talks/S27E08_Video.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely warm and practically grounded talk that weaves climate anxiety into the spiral path with memorable, down-to-earth examples (the cooling fizz of novelty becoming tranquility is a particularly fine reframing), while the sequenced entry points and calibrated low-bar advice ('small is beautiful') give practitioners clear, actionable footholds — minor weaknesses include some looseness in distinguishing the entry points as a coherent system and occasional conceptual slippage between rapture-as-jhāna-factor and rapture-as-curiosity, but neither undermines the overall integrity of the instruction.

dharma_talks/S27E09_2023_Oct_29_The_Spir.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E09_2023_Oct_29_The_Spir.title: 2023 Oct 29 The Spiral Path
dharma_talks/S27E09_2023_Oct_29_The_Spir.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warmly grounded and practically useful exploration of the Upanisā Sutta's spiral path, with memorable phenomenological observations (tranquillity hidden within deflation, rapture as simple curiosity) and genuine pastoral warmth, while remaining doctrinally faithful to dependent origination and the jhāna factors; minor weaknesses include a somewhat loose framing of the seven 'entry points' that slightly blurs the sutta's own structure, and the climate-change framing, though evocative, occasionally risks instrumentalising dukkha in ways that need more careful nuance.
dharma_talks/S27E09_2023_Oct_29_The_Spir.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warmly authentic, practically grounded talk that skillfully maps abstract spiral-path stages onto vivid everyday scenarios (climate anxiety, dishwashing, sunsets), making the sequence genuinely motivating and actionable, while the careful sequencing of links and the repeated 'small is beautiful' calibration keep the instructions honest and safe to follow — minor weaknesses being occasional looseness in distinguishing overlapping terms (gladness vs. rapture vs. happiness) and a slightly abrupt ending that leaves the upper spiral less fully developed.

dharma_talks/S27E10_2021_Four_Noble_Trut.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E10_2021_Four_Noble_Trut.title: 2021 Four Noble Truths
dharma_talks/S27E10_2021_Four_Noble_Trut.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personally authentic overview of the Four Noble Truths with genuinely moving moments—the Mae Chee Kaew quotation, the nibbanic gap framing, and the U Pandita anecdote—yet the talk is doctrinally uneven in places (the three types of dukkha are conflated rather than clearly distinguished, the claim that an arahant still has greed and anger arise is asserted without the standard vipassanā-kilesa nuance, and the suggestion that 'something that doesn't die' resides 'within' risks sounding like an ātman view without careful qualification), making it an inspiring but imprecise introduction that rewards engaged listeners but could mislead beginners on key technical points.
dharma_talks/S27E10_2021_Four_Noble_Trut.craft_reason: The talk is genuinely warm and moving — the Mae Chee Kaew closing, the Sayadaw U Pandita anecdote, and the 'nibbanic gap' framing are memorable and inspiring — while remaining practically grounded in meditation instruction, though the structural flow across the Four Noble Truths is somewhat loose and the third and fourth truths receive uneven treatment, limiting its score on craft.

dharma_talks/S27E11_Dukkha_Unsatisfactor.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E11_Dukkha_Unsatisfactor.title: Dukkha (Unsatisfactoriness and Sila (Morality and Ethics) -
dharma_talks/S27E11_Dukkha_Unsatisfactor.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, conversational and doctrinally grounded tour through dukkha, sila, the kilesas, and anusaya—faithful to Theravāda teaching with nice touches on latent tendencies and prejudice—but the talk is loosely structured, the meditation instructions are thin, and while it is engaging and authentic it rarely rises to genuinely moving or memorable.
dharma_talks/S27E11_Dukkha_Unsatisfactor.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, an engaged conversational voice, and illuminating moments—especially on latent tendencies/anusaya and prejudice—but its inspiration is diluted by loose, list-driven structure and several underdeveloped threads, while its craft suffers from inconsistent term usage, incomplete sequencing between topics (sila, kilesas, anusaya never fully integrate), and meditation instructions that are suggestive rather than precise, yielding a talk that is solidly useful but falls short of outstanding on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S27E12_Dependent_Originatio.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E12_Dependent_Originatio.title: Dependent Origination, the Role of desire and the only Choice.
dharma_talks/S27E12_Dependent_Originatio.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, experienced, and doctrinally grounded walkthrough of dependent origination—with the ice-cream identity sequence and the crossroads analogy offering genuinely memorable pedagogical moments—but the talk is somewhat truncated and self-referential (noting it is a re-recording), the treatment of taṇhā and the 'only moment of free will' framing is suggestive but underexplored, and while technically sound in its broad strokes, it lacks the precision and depth that would lift it into the outstanding range on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S27E12_Dependent_Originatio.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, a clear and well-sequenced walk through dependent origination with a memorable ice-cream illustration and the 'only moment of free will' insight, but it remains conversational and somewhat meandering rather than truly galvanizing, and the practical meditation instructions—while present and broadly usable—are brief and loosely integrated into the conceptual framework.

dharma_talks/S27E13_2022_Oct_09_Identity.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S27E13_2022_Oct_09_Identity.title: 2022 Oct 09 Identity and Not-Self.
dharma_talks/S27E13_2022_Oct_09_Identity.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely moving and technically grounded talk: the personal anecdotes (gas canister, printer cartridge, emotional storm) are vivid and self-deprecatingly honest, the internal/external mindfulness framework drawn from Satipaṭṭhāna is applied with care, and the progression from role-identification through upādāna to a lived glimpse of anattā is both pedagogically clear and doctrinally faithful—minor weaknesses include the 'disembodied hovering observer' language which, while experientially described, risks being taken as a subtle-self view without stronger corrective framing, and the Pema Chödrön citation (a Tibetan teacher) sits unremarked in a Theravāda context, but neither flaw seriously undermines a talk that is simultaneously warm, rigorous, and genuinely inspiring toward practice.
dharma_talks/S27E13_2022_Oct_09_Identity.craft_reason: The talk is genuinely moving and well-crafted, anchored in an honest, self-deprecating personal narrative that makes anattā viscerally real, with clear internal/external mindfulness framing and practically followable vipassanā instruction, though the meditation mechanics shift somewhat loosely between metaphor and technique and the mirror-image passage, while poetic, briefly loses instructional precision.

dharma_talks/S28E01_Video.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S28E01_Video.title: Video
dharma_talks/S28E01_Video.full_reason: The talk is warm, conversational, and carries genuine personal authenticity with some memorable anecdotes (the jazz club, the cooking course, the Carroll quote), but it meanders without strong doctrinal anchoring—the reframe of 'right livelihood' as 'right lifestyle' is reasonable but handled loosely, the treatment of the five wrong livelihoods is superficial and hedged, and the promising Ānanda/kalyāṇamittatā passage is not developed into a coherent argument, leaving the talk doctrinally thin and inspirationally pleasant but not particularly stirring.
dharma_talks/S28E01_Video.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, conversational, and at times genuinely charming talk — the jazz anecdote and the Ānanda exchange are memorable — but the overall arc is discursive and loosely structured, the reframing of right livelihood as 'right lifestyle' is suggestive yet underdeveloped, and the talk contains no meditation instruction, making its practical actionability thin despite its accessibility and authenticity.

dharma_talks/S28E02_Right_Livelihood.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S28E02_Right_Livelihood.title: Right Livelihood
dharma_talks/S28E02_Right_Livelihood.full_reason: The talk is warm, personable, and rich with relatable anecdotes and the useful reframing of right livelihood as 'right lifestyle,' but it is doctrinally thin—the Upaddha Sutta reference is used loosely, the treatment of the five wrong trades is cursory and hedged, and the conceptual leap from kalyāṇamittatā to livelihood is not carefully argued—leaving it an agreeable but intellectually undemanding reflection rather than a fully sound or deeply inspiring dharma teaching.
dharma_talks/S28E02_Right_Livelihood.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, charming personal anecdotes, and a thoughtful expansion of right livelihood into 'right lifestyle,' but it meanders without a clear structure, the meditation/practice instructions are virtually absent, and the conceptual development stays surface-level throughout, leaving it solid but unremarkable on both dimensions.

dharma_talks/S28E03_2022_Sep_11_Rest_for.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S28E03_2022_Sep_11_Rest_for.title: 2022 Sep 11 Rest for Autumn.
dharma_talks/S28E03_2022_Sep_11_Rest_for.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practically grounded and gently humorous talk with genuinely useful daily-practice guidance and doctrinally sound framing of vipassanā, anattā, and mettā, but the instruction remains fairly general and conversational rather than precise or memorable enough to rank as outstanding on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S28E03_2022_Sep_11_Rest_for.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's warm, conversational voice and practical framing of a full day's practice arc are genuinely engaging and accessible, but the talk's relaxed, meandering structure and occasional vagueness in vipassanā instruction (the distancing/anattā move is underdeveloped; the sequence from calm to investigation could be clearer) keep it from reaching the top tier on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S29E01_Bahiya_of_the_Bark_C.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S29E01_Bahiya_of_the_Bark_C.title: Bahiya of the Bark Cloth
dharma_talks/S29E01_Bahiya_of_the_Bark_C.full_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, wit, and a compelling framing of the Bāhiya sutta through the Upaniṣadic bark-cloth connection, but the doctrinal exposition of the key formula ('neither here nor beyond nor in between') is somewhat loose and incomplete, the hagiographical asides dilute rather than deepen the teaching, and the explanation stops just short of giving the listener a clear, practically actionable understanding of what 'merely the seen' actually means in practice.
dharma_talks/S29E01_Bahiya_of_the_Bark_C.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, dry wit, and an interesting contextual framing linking the Upanishadic seer-tradition to Bahiya, but the core meditation instruction on 'merely the seen' is only partially unpacked—the explanation of how to actually train in this way remains abstract and incomplete—leaving the talk intellectually engaging but neither reliably inspiring nor fully actionable as practice guidance.

dharma_talks/S29E02_2023_March_05.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S29E02_2023_March_05.title: 2023 March 05
dharma_talks/S29E02_2023_March_05.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, learned, and genuinely engaging reading of the Bāhiya Sutta with memorable digressions and authentic voice, but the doctrinal exposition is uneven—the gloss on 'you will not be with that / in that' as pointing to 'something distinct from everything we experience' risks implying a witnessing self, and the treatment of Nibbāna wavers between the two views without firmly anchoring the anattā principle, leaving the soundness solid but meaningfully short of rigorous.
dharma_talks/S29E02_2023_March_05.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma brings genuine warmth, scholarly texture, and a lovely narrative arc through the Bāhiya story, with moments of real inspiration, but the meditation instruction remains conceptually suggestive rather than practically actionable, and the key passage—'in the seen merely what is seen'—is explained through philosophical abstraction rather than clear, sequenced practice guidance a meditator could directly follow.

dharma_talks/S29E03_.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S29E03_.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, well-grounded retelling of MN 56 with genuine authenticity, accurate doctrinal framing of cetanā and kamma, and charming storytelling that holds the listener's interest, though the talk stays largely narrative and expository rather than probing the teaching's implications deeply enough to be truly galvanizing, and the practical/contemplative payoff at the close feels somewhat abrupt given the richness of the sutta.
dharma_talks/S29E03_.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, conversational retelling of a genuinely interesting sutta with moments of real charm and dry wit (the 'removing testicles' exchange lands well), but the talk stays largely at the level of narrative summary rather than offering precise meditation instruction or rigorous conceptual development of cetanā, leaving it engaging and accessible without being either deeply moving or technically precise enough to score higher on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S30E01_2022_Aug_14_Climate_.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S30E01_2022_Aug_14_Climate_.title: 2022 Aug 14 Climate Emergency and the Role of the Dhamma Video
dharma_talks/S30E01_2022_Aug_14_Climate_.full_reason: The talk shows genuine pastoral warmth and courage in addressing a difficult topic, grounded by a well-chosen sutta citation and a sound pivot toward spiritual equanimity, but it meanders through political commentary and anecdote without disciplined dhamma structure, and its doctrinal content—while not wrong—remains thin and underdeveloped relative to the gravity of the subject.
dharma_talks/S30E01_2022_Aug_14_Climate_.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, moral urgency, and a memorable sutta reading, but it meanders across political commentary, climate statistics, and personal anecdotes without weaving them into coherent, actionable practice guidance—leaving it emotionally engaging in patches yet too unfocused and light on practical instruction to score strongly on either dimension.

dharma_talks/S30E02_Non-Violence_v_Pacif.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S30E02_Non-Violence_v_Pacif.title: Non-Violence v. Pacifism
dharma_talks/S30E02_Non-Violence_v_Pacif.full_reason: The talk offers genuine warmth, vivid illustrations (the samurai, the Chakravartin myth, the Pārājika origin story), and a practically useful force/violence distinction, but its inspiration is undercut by a discursive, somewhat rambling structure and an inconclusive treatment of the Ukraine context, while its soundness, though generally faithful to Theravāda sources, contains a slight overreach in claiming the Buddha's society was entirely preliterate and a somewhat unguarded assertion that killing without hatred 'comes under non-violence,' which the Abhidhamma caveat only partially redeems.
dharma_talks/S30E02_Non-Violence_v_Pacif.craft_reason: The talk offers genuinely interesting conceptual work distinguishing force from violence and grounding non-violence in experiential ethics rather than ideology, with some memorable illustrative moments (the samurai story, the mobile phone analogy), but it meanders without a clear structure, the practical payoff for a meditator is thin, and the meditation-instruction craft is essentially absent, leaving it intellectually stimulating but neither deeply moving nor reliably actionable as practice guidance.

dharma_talks/S30E03_2022_Apr_17_Nolibera.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S30E03_2022_Apr_17_Nolibera.title: 2022 Apr 17 Noliberalism and Mindfulness
dharma_talks/S30E03_2022_Apr_17_Nolibera.full_reason: The talk is warm and earnest, with a genuinely inspiring closing on dāna and the Buddha quote on generosity, but its socio-political commentary is too discursive and only loosely tethered to canonical Theravāda doctrine, while the equation of neoliberalism with 'Mara's work' and the Mara narrative are simplified, and the practical meditation/ethical guidance remains thin and imprecise.
dharma_talks/S30E03_2022_Apr_17_Nolibera.craft_reason: The talk delivers genuine warmth, a sharp sociopolitical critique, and a memorable closing quote on generosity that can genuinely move listeners, but it functions more as a discursive social commentary than a meditation or practice talk—offering almost no actionable meditation instruction, loose conceptual transitions between economics and Dhamma, and a somewhat meandering structure that limits its practical usefulness and overall craft score.

dharma_talks/S30E04_2022_Jun_19_Social_C.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S30E04_2022_Jun_19_Social_C.title: 2022 Jun 19 Social Conditionng or Karma - Our social conditioning is a given, but even so we have to take responsibility for it and cleanse it any unwholesomeness.
dharma_talks/S30E04_2022_Jun_19_Social_C.full_reason: The talk offers an engaging, warmly personal exploration of social conditioning with good doctrinal grounding (kamma as intentional action, the Ānanda/kalyāṇamitta passage, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta on the Vajjis, Sigālovāda Sutta), but the delivery is discursive and anecdote-heavy rather than truly energizing, the distinction between social conditioning and kamma could be drawn more rigorously, and the practical guidance for actually working with unwholesome conditioning in practice is largely absent, leaving the talk doctrinally adequate but insufficiently precise or inspiring to score higher.
dharma_talks/S30E04_2022_Jun_19_Social_C.craft_reason: The talk offers warm, candid personal anecdotes and a genuinely useful distinction between social karma and social conditioning, but it meanders through political commentary without clear meditation instruction or practical steps, leaving both its inspirational arc and its craft somewhat underdelivered.

dharma_talks/S31E01_Buddha_Day_Address_H.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E01_Buddha_Day_Address_H.title: Buddha Day Address : His Training : The Fetters
dharma_talks/S31E01_Buddha_Day_Address_H.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, learned, and often vivid Buddha Day address—the lightning/starry-night/full-moon/noonday-sun simile for the four attainments is genuinely memorable, the sutta quotations are well-chosen, and the personal asides add authentic warmth—while remaining doctrinally solid on the fetters, the three knowledges, and anattā, though a few claims are imprecise (describing the cūḷa-sotāpanna status as commentary-derived without flagging its limited canonical authority, slightly blurring the distinction between āsavā and saṃyojana, and conflating 'defilements' with a broad structural ignorance in ways that could confuse a careful student), keeping it in the strong-but-not-outstanding range on both dimensions.
dharma_talks/S31E01_Buddha_Day_Address_H.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's talk is warm, learned, and often vivid—the sutta quotations land with real force, the fetter-as-shackle framing is clear and practically actionable, and flashes of dry humor humanise the teaching—but inspiration is tempered by a somewhat rambling middle section and the soundness is slightly uneven: the progression through the four stages and ten fetters is generally crisp, yet the treatment of the three characteristics feels rushed and loosely sequenced, leaving a practitioner without quite enough to act on in those moments.

dharma_talks/S31E02_ood_Friendhship_Good.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E02_ood_Friendhship_Good.title: ood Friendhship, Good Companionship, Good Comradeship - Ubuntu
dharma_talks/S31E02_ood_Friendhship_Good.full_reason: A warm, wide-ranging, and genuinely charming talk with strong narrative energy—the Ubuntu framing, the feral-child story, the dog-duty sutta, and the proprioception digression are all memorable—but the loose associative structure, occasional doctrinal imprecision (e.g., treating awareness-as-empty as a casual aside, the somewhat muddled free-will remark), and lack of rigorous meditation instruction prevent it from reaching the highest tier on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S31E02_ood_Friendhship_Good.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, discursive, and humanly engaging talk with genuinely memorable touches—the feral child story, Ubuntu, osmosis, the dog-ascetic passage—that make the central relational insight stick, but the talk wanders considerably without crisp structural payoff, and while the Satipaṭṭhāna framing (internal/external/both) is sound as a practical lens, it is introduced late and never fully developed into actionable instruction, leaving the craft slightly under-realized relative to the inspirational warmth.

dharma_talks/S31E03_Dependent_Originatio.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E03_Dependent_Originatio.title: Dependent Origination Revisited
dharma_talks/S31E03_Dependent_Originatio.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, experienced, and genuinely engaging walkthrough of dependent origination with memorable analogies (tongue-biting, ice cream button, consumer excitement vs. contentment) and authentic practitioner voice, but the talk's casual, associative structure leads to occasional doctrinal looseness—most notably the ambiguous framing of viññāṇa as a passive 'screen' without adequately distinguishing the various citta functions, a somewhat idiosyncratic rendering of avijjā as mere 'not knowing' that softens its active delusive force, and the sūnyatā digression that blurs Theravāda/Mahāyāna distinctions—resulting in a talk that is warmly inspiring and broadly sound but not rigorous enough to score in the outstanding tier on either dimension.
dharma_talks/S31E03_Dependent_Originatio.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, learned, and often genuinely illuminating talk — the tongue-in-the-door identity example, the whirlpool moment of grasping, and the consumer-excitement-versus-happiness distinction are memorable and alive — but the talk meanders significantly (the Schweitzer digression, the parking anecdote, the forgotten word), and while the dependent origination sequence is clearly sequenced, the meditation instructions proper are thin and underspecified, leaving a practitioner with rich conceptual framing but limited actionable guidance.

dharma_talks/S31E04_Karma-_Specific_Cond.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E04_Karma-_Specific_Cond.title: Karma- Specific, Conditionality the Five Laws, ethical behaviour, social karma-Neoliberalism.
dharma_talks/S31E04_Karma-_Specific_Cond.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warmly authentic and wide-ranging talk with genuinely memorable passages—the thermal underwear generosity teaching, the Pascal's wager adaptation, the samurai story—and real inspirational energy around ethics and interconnection, but doctrinal soundness is undermined by a muddled presentation of the five niyāmas (the fifth is listed as dhamma rather than the standard dhamma-niyāma, and karma's own category is nearly skipped), the causal claim that 'the suffering comes because of that reaction' risks misreading vedanā and paṭicca-samuppāda in ways that could inadvertently blame trauma survivors, and the extended neoliberalism digression, while thought-provoking, is doctrinally thin and crowds out the careful Buddhist analysis the topic deserves.
dharma_talks/S31E04_Karma-_Specific_Cond.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's warmth, personal anecdotes, and the sweep from conditionality through social karma to war give the talk genuine inspirational energy and memorable moments, but the structural looseness—long neoliberalism digression, abrupt topic shifts, underdeveloped meditation instructions, and inconsistent handling of the five niyāmas—undermines the craft soundness enough to cap the overall score in the solid-but-uneven range.

dharma_talks/S31E05_No_more_ideologies.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E05_No_more_ideologies.title: No more ideologies!
dharma_talks/S31E05_No_more_ideologies.full_reason: The talk is genuinely engaging and culturally wide-ranging, with Bhante Bodhidhamma's warmth and wit carrying a compelling critique of modern ideologies toward a Dhamma-grounded ethics of community, but the doctrinal content is thin and loosely applied—the Vajji passages and brahmavihāra references are handled competently but not rigorously, the central teaching on anattā and samsāra is sketched rather than developed, and the connection between the political analysis and the Buddha's actual path remains underdeveloped, leaving both the inspiration and soundness solidly good but short of outstanding.
dharma_talks/S31E05_No_more_ideologies.craft_reason: The talk is genuinely engaging and intellectually stimulating — the sweep from neoliberalism to the Vajji sutta is memorable and the Rushkoff anecdote lands with real force — but it is primarily a socio-political essay with Buddhist framing bolted on rather than integrated, lacks meditation instruction or actionable practice guidance, and the conceptual bridge from ideology-critique to Buddhist ethics is asserted rather than carefully built, leaving the 'craft soundness' dimension noticeably thin.

dharma_talks/S31E06_The_Mahasi_Technique.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E06_The_Mahasi_Technique.title: The Mahasi Technique and What We Need to Understand to Practice Vipassana.
dharma_talks/S31E06_The_Mahasi_Technique.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practical, and often vivid talk—the Narcissus image, the child-and-spider illustration, the rugby player facing death—that genuinely motivates practice, while the doctrinal and technical content is broadly sound (correct treatment of noting, intention, the three characteristics, hindrances, anattā), though occasional imprecisions (the description of Nibbāna as 'the awareness experiencing its own true nature' edges toward an ātman-adjacent framing, and the developmental psychology of the infant is used loosely) prevent it from reaching the highest tier.
dharma_talks/S31E06_The_Mahasi_Technique.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a genuinely warm and intellectually alive talk, with memorable images (Narcissus, the child and the spider, the stone-throwing analogy, the rugby player facing death) and an authentic, unhurried voice that draws the listener toward practice, while the meditation instructions are clearly sequenced, practically actionable, and conceptually coherent, though occasional looseness in transitions and an informal rambling quality keep both dimensions just short of outstanding.

dharma_talks/S31E07_Dependent_Orignation.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dharma_talks/S31E07_Dependent_Orignation.title: Dependent Orignation and how all other importnant teachings are included.

dhammabytes/S01E02_02_Discourse_to_the_K.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and accessible framing of the Kalama Sutta, with some memorable moments (communism and Nazism from rationality, the dying Buddha's instruction), but it reads largely as a sutta recitation with light commentary rather than a crafted dharma talk—the metta practice is introduced but not explained or made actionable, the conceptual exploration of 'how do we know truth' is left somewhat unresolved, and the overall structure trails off rather than building toward a clear, inspiring conclusion.

dhammabytes/S01E03_03_Desire_the_Root_of.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S01E03_03_Desire_the_Root_of.title: 03 Desire the Root of Suffering
dhammabytes/S01E03_03_Desire_the_Root_of.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, pedagogically astute talk that skillfully traces the Second Noble Truth through a concrete sutta, reinforces tanha versus wholesome desire with reasonable nuance, and offers a genuinely evocative lectio-style practice suggestion—though the inspirational arc is gentle rather than stirring, and a few minor imprecisions (e.g., collapsing 'desire' into tanha without fully distinguishing chanda, and slightly loose framing of osmotic absorption as a meditation method) keep both scores from reaching the outstanding tier.
dhammabytes/S01E03_03_Desire_the_Root_of.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, lucid, and practically grounded talk that builds genuine insight through skillful repetition and real-world analogy, but it is modest in scope—more a guided reflection than a fully developed meditation instruction—and while the lectio-style digestion technique is a genuinely useful practical tool, the talk's craft is conversational rather than rigorously structured, leaving it strong but not outstanding on either dimension.

dhammabytes/S01E04_04_How_to_Test_the_Bu.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S01E04_04_How_to_Test_the_Bu.title: 04 How to Test the Buddha
dhammabytes/S01E04_04_How_to_Test_the_Bu.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a doctrinally faithful and thoughtful walk through a genuine sutta on testing the Tathāgata—grounded in the text, helpfully illustrated by the Ajahn Chah anecdote, and ending with an appropriately humble exhortation—but the delivery is discursive and meandering rather than truly energising, the translation commentary on 'Tathāgata' is speculative and slightly muddled, and the talk never quite builds the momentum or evocative imagery needed to leave listeners deeply moved or urgently inspired toward practice.
dhammabytes/S01E04_04_How_to_Test_the_Bu.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a thoughtful, unhurried reading of the Vīmaṃsaka Sutta with genuine warmth and the Ajahn Chah anecdote lands memorably, but the talk functions primarily as a sutta recitation with light commentary rather than as crafted inspiration or sequenced instruction, leaving both emotional momentum and practical takeaways somewhat underdeveloped.

dhammabytes/S02E01_01_Introducing_the_Bu.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S02E01_01_Introducing_the_Bu.title: 01 Introducing the Buddha
dhammabytes/S02E01_01_Introducing_the_Bu.full_reason: A warm, accessible introductory talk with genuine authenticity and useful contextual framing, but it meanders through cultural history, rebirth anecdotes, and textual commentary without building sustained momentum or depth, while doctrinal explanations (Tathāgata etymology, Kalama Sutta summary, the four paths) are broadly accurate yet occasionally imprecise or oversimplified, leaving both inspiration and soundness solidly competent but unremarkable.
dhammabytes/S02E01_01_Introducing_the_Bu.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, scholarly breadth, and some memorable moments (the etymology of 'anukampanā', the student who couldn't accept transcendence), but it meanders through historical, doctrinal, and anecdotal material without a clear arc, offers almost no actionable meditation instruction, and the conceptual transitions are loose enough to limit both its inspirational impact and its practical usefulness.

dhammabytes/S02E02_02_The_Birth_of_the_B.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S02E02_02_The_Birth_of_the_B.title: 02 The Birth of the Buddha
dhammabytes/S02E02_02_The_Birth_of_the_B.full_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and an engaging conversational style, and its culminating pivot to the Tathāgata's mindful awareness of feelings/perceptions/thoughts as the Buddha's true 'marvellous quality' is doctrinally apt and well-framed, but it is undermined by a loose six-realms enumeration (omitting or mislabelling realms), a casual and slightly misleading treatment of the Bodhisattva concept (conflating Theravāda and Mahāyāna usage), and anecdotal digressions (Nisargadatta, New Guinea birth) that dilute rather than deepen the teaching, leaving it solid but unremarkable on both inspiration and soundness.
dhammabytes/S02E02_02_The_Birth_of_the_B.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and some memorable moments—the cinematic birth narrative, the unexpected New Guinea anecdote, the final pivot to bare awareness as the Buddha's true wonder—but it meanders through historical digressions and cosmological asides without tight structure, and the meditation/practice dimension is almost entirely absent, leaving a practitioner with little concrete to act on.

dhammabytes/S02E03_03_The_Bodhisatta_Lea.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S02E03_03_The_Bodhisatta_Lea.title: 03 The Bodhisatta Leaves Home
dhammabytes/S02E03_03_The_Bodhisatta_Lea.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, learned, and doctrinally faithful walk through the Ariyapariyesanā Sutta—correctly distinguishing the arūpajhānas from Nibbāna, handling the bodhisatta's five faculties accurately, and thoughtfully correcting the misreading that the Buddha condemned lay life—but the talk is more scholarly commentary than inspirational exhortation, with only occasional moments of real rhetorical lift, making it solid and trustworthy rather than genuinely moving.
dhammabytes/S02E03_03_The_Bodhisatta_Lea.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, wit, and a strong narrative thread that makes the Bodhisatta's quest feel alive and personally relevant, but the meditation instruction on the arūpajhānas, while earnest, is loosely sequenced and imprecise, and the talk occasionally wanders (the St. Francis aside, the serf etymology) in ways that dilute rather than deepen the central theme, leaving it solidly engaging but short of outstanding on either dimension.

dhammabytes/S02E04_04_The_Essence_of_the.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S02E04_04_The_Essence_of_the.title: 04 The Essence of the Awakening
dhammabytes/S02E04_04_The_Essence_of_the.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a doctrinally faithful and clearly explained walk through dependent origination with the evocative ancient-city simile landing well, but the delivery is discursive and understated rather than truly moving, and the treatment of the consciousness/nāmarūpa loop—while broadly correct—stays at a surface level without the conceptual precision or meditative depth that would make it both technically rigorous and genuinely inspiring.
dhammabytes/S02E04_04_The_Essence_of_the.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth and engages meaningfully with the dependent origination teaching, anchored by a lovely simile, but it functions more as a discursive commentary on scripture than a crafted dharma talk — meditation instruction is essentially absent, conceptual explanations (especially the consciousness/name-form loop) remain somewhat impressionistic, and the structure feels loosely assembled rather than purposefully built toward a practical or transformative takeaway.

dhammabytes/S03E01_Anusaya_-_Latent_Tend.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E01_Anusaya_-_Latent_Tend.title: Anusaya - Latent Tendencies
dhammabytes/S03E01_Anusaya_-_Latent_Tend.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a competent, warm, and doctrinally grounded overview of the seven anusaya with useful structural reordering around ignorance, but the talk is too brief and exploratory to be deeply moving, the computer analogy is only partially apt and acknowledged as limited, and while the core Abhidhamma and dependent-origination framing is sound, the casual hedging ('I think,' 'sort of') and underdeveloped practical guidance keep both inspiration and doctrinal precision at a solid but unremarkable level.
dhammabytes/S03E01_Anusaya_-_Latent_Tend.craft_reason: The talk offers a genuinely interesting conceptual map of the anusaya with a warm, conversational voice and a clever computer analogy, but it remains largely intellectual and expository — it neither moves the listener toward practice nor provides actionable meditation guidance, leaving it solid but unremarkable on both dimensions.

dhammabytes/S03E02_Asava-Taints_Ogha-Flo.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E02_Asava-Taints_Ogha-Flo.title: Asava-Taints, Ogha-Floods, Yoga-Yokes
dhammabytes/S03E02_Asava-Taints_Ogha-Flo.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's talk is a competent, warmly delivered etymological survey of āsava with accurate core doctrinal content (the four āsavas, their link to the fetters and stages of awakening, khīṇāsava), but it reads as a loosely structured lecture rather than an inspiring dharma talk—occasional hedging ('I don't quite understand that'), meandering asides, and the absence of narrative, embodied imagery, or practice guidance keep both inspiration and depth from rising above the solid-but-unremarkable range.
dhammabytes/S03E02_Asava-Taints_Ogha-Flo.craft_reason: The talk offers genuine scholarly warmth and some vivid etymological texture (the oozing sore, the flood, the yoke), but it remains a fairly dry definitional survey with loose structure, occasional conceptual muddiness (the influx/outflow ambiguity unresolved, the moha/avijjā distinction asserted but not clearly unpacked), and no meditation instructions or clear practical takeaways — leaving it solid but unremarkable on both inspiration and craft.

dhammabytes/S03E03_Buddha.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E03_Buddha.title: Buddha
dhammabytes/S03E03_Buddha.full_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, dry wit, and devotional authenticity that make the nine Buddha-qualities memorable and approachable, but it contains a few doctrinal imprecisions—most notably equating arahatship with 'Sāvaka Buddha' (a non-standard conflation), the casual dismissal of the Buddha's continuing existence ('obviously it doesn't exist'), and some loose handling of Paccekabuddha doctrine—that prevent it from scoring high on soundness, keeping the overall from reaching the outstanding range despite its considerable inspirational charm.
dhammabytes/S03E03_Buddha.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma's warm, witty voice and charming asides (the dull monk story, the cup-of-tea joke) make the nine Buddha-qualities genuinely engaging, but the talk is more an appreciative survey than practical instruction—meditation guidance is brief and loosely framed—and several conceptual points (e.g. conflating arahant with 'Sāvaka Buddha,' the offhand dismissal of the cloth exercise) are imprecise enough to limit both its craft soundness and its ability to move a practitioner toward concrete action.

dhammabytes/S03E04_Dukkha_-_A_Hard_Place.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E04_Dukkha_-_A_Hard_Place.title: Dukkha - A Hard Place
dhammabytes/S03E04_Dukkha_-_A_Hard_Place.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, accessible, and doctrinally grounded survey of the three kinds of dukkha with good practical grounding, but the talk remains somewhat discursive and conversational rather than deeply moving, and contains a few imprecisions (e.g., equating dukkha-dukkha primarily with 'emotional stuff' while downplaying physical pain, and the slightly muddled claim that saṅkhāra-dukkha is solely about the delusion of self rather than the conditioned nature of formations), keeping both scores solidly in the competent-but-unremarkable range.
dhammabytes/S03E04_Dukkha_-_A_Hard_Place.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, accessible, and at times genuinely evocative exploration of dukkha—the etymology, three types, and link to daily life are clearly sequenced and practically grounded—but the talk remains largely discursive and explanatory rather than truly moving, the transition to meditative application is brief and underdeveloped, and occasional imprecisions (e.g., collapsing dukkha-dukkha into 'emotional stuff' while excluding physical pain inconsistently) limit both its inspirational lift and its technical sharpness.

dhammabytes/S03E05_Hetu_-_The_Unwholesom.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E05_Hetu_-_The_Unwholesom.title: Hetu - The Unwholesome Roots
dhammabytes/S03E05_Hetu_-_The_Unwholesom.full_reason: A genuinely thoughtful and experientially grounded talk that explains the three unwholesome roots with psychological depth and an authentic, personal voice (the gate story is nicely humanizing), and is broadly doctrinally sound in its treatment of lobha, dosa, moha, anattā, and the liberating function of vipassanā awareness, though it is somewhat brief and loosely structured, the practical meditation guidance is light rather than rigorous, and the closing gesture toward dependent origination feels abrupt rather than integrated.
dhammabytes/S03E05_Hetu_-_The_Unwholesom.craft_reason: A warm, clearly voiced talk with a genuinely illuminating psychological framing of the three roots — especially the gate anecdote and the 'fear of fear' passage — but it remains somewhat discursive and under-structured, with meditation instructions more gestured at than sequenced, leaving it solid and thought-provoking rather than deeply moving or precisely actionable.

dhammabytes/S03E06_Panya_-_Wisdom_and_In.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E06_Panya_-_Wisdom_and_In.title: Panya - Wisdom and Intuitive Intelligence
dhammabytes/S03E06_Panya_-_Wisdom_and_In.full_reason: The talk offers genuinely evocative framing of paññā as intuitive intelligence—with warm, unpretentious delivery and memorable analogies (tongue tasting curry, sleeping on a problem)—but is undermined doctrinally by the conflation of paññā with a 'primordial intelligence' or 'Buddha nature' that sounds more Mahāyāna/Dzogchen than Theravāda, the imprecise etymology of paññā, and the loose equation of sati and paññā (satipaññā) as a compound pointing to 'awareness-intelligence,' which blurs a distinction the Pali Nikāyas treat carefully.
dhammabytes/S03E06_Panya_-_Wisdom_and_In.craft_reason: The talk has genuine warmth, memorable analogies (tongue tasting itself, sleeping on a problem, the tennis player), and an authentically exploratory voice that invites investigation, but the meditation instruction is sparse and loosely sequenced—the core claim about 'disembedding intelligence from body, heart and mind' is never translated into concrete, actionable practice steps, leaving the craft dimension competent but insufficiently rigorous for a practitioner to act on reliably.

dhammabytes/S03E07_Puja_-_Devotional_Att.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E07_Puja_-_Devotional_Att.title: Puja - Devotional Attention
dhammabytes/S03E07_Puja_-_Devotional_Att.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personally flavored and genuinely instructive talk on puja that is rich in devotional texture and practical symbolism, with mostly sound Theravāda framing, but the casual digressions (e.g., the dismissal of polyphonic music as 'silly,' the slightly muddled mudra descriptions, and the brief conflation of the Bodhi-tree/footprint tradition's timeline) introduce minor inaccuracies and reduce both doctrinal precision and the inspirational lift needed to score higher.
dhammabytes/S03E07_Puja_-_Devotional_Att.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma brings genuine warmth, memorable images (the merry-go-round, the candle's heat and light, Gregorian chant corrupted by romantics), and an authentic contemplative voice that makes the devotional dimension of practice feel alive and necessary, but the talk is structurally loose—moving associatively from mudras to music to stupas to refuge without clear sequencing—and the practical guidance, while evocative, rarely sharpens into precise, actionable instruction a practitioner could reliably follow.

dhammabytes/S03E08_Samyojana_-_The_first.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E08_Samyojana_-_The_first.title: Samyojana - The first three Fetters
dhammabytes/S03E08_Samyojana_-_The_first.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, personally grounded and doctrinally faithful account of the first three fetters and their connection to stream-entry, with memorable practical touches (the lightning-flash simile, the meditation-technique-as-ritual insight), though the talk is conversational rather than deeply moving and contains minor imprecisions (e.g., the casual gloss of 'Ehi Passiko' and the speculative previous-life explanation for variation in stream-entry experience) that slightly undercut its doctrinal tightness without seriously misleading.
dhammabytes/S03E08_Samyojana_-_The_first.craft_reason: The talk offers warm, accessible, and occasionally vivid explanation of the first three fetters with genuine practitioner authenticity and useful nuance (e.g., the ritual discussion, the variability of sotāpatti experience), but it lacks memorable imagery or narrative drive to be truly moving, and the conceptual exposition, while clear, meanders without tight sequencing, leaving a practitioner with good orientation but limited actionable instruction.

dhammabytes/S03E09_Samyojana_-_The_last_.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E09_Samyojana_-_The_last_.title: Samyojana - The last seven Fetters
dhammabytes/S03E09_Samyojana_-_The_last_.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, experienced voice with genuinely evocative images (bobbing head, swimming to the island, ice cream analogy for jhāna attachment) and an honest, practitioner-grounded tone that inspires reflection, but the talk is somewhat loosely structured, the treatment of the higher fetters (especially conceit and restlessness) is impressionistic rather than rigorous, the claim that 'all comparison is odious' slightly oversimplifies māna, and a few doctrinal details (e.g. attributing the lighting/moon imagery sequence directly to the Buddha without qualification, the anāgāmī's relation to rūpa-jhāna fetters) are stated with more confidence than the textual evidence warrants, keeping both scores solidly competent but short of outstanding.
dhammabytes/S03E09_Samyojana_-_The_last_.craft_reason: The talk offers genuinely warm, memorable images (bobbing heads, island swim, ice cream for jhāna) and an authentic voice that orients the listener toward practice, while the doctrinal mapping of the fetters is reasonably clear and the paradox of effortless effort is well-framed, though the structure is somewhat loose, a few key terms (conceit vs. self, restlessness) are explained imprecisely, and the practical meditation guidance is sparse rather than actionable.

dhammabytes/S03E10_Sati_-_Knowing.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E10_Sati_-_Knowing.title: Sati - Knowing
dhammabytes/S03E10_Sati_-_Knowing.full_reason: The talk is genuinely warm and evocative—the image of the child discovering the butterfly, the gerund 'knowing,' the 'stop' instruction are all memorable and point skillfully toward practice—but doctrinal precision slips in several places: conflating vipassanā with jhāna as 'vipassanā absorptions,' the claim that the original delusion is specifically 'the belief that we are human beings' (an uncanonical framing), and the phrase 'that's our Buddha nature' (a Mahāyāna concept foreign to Theravāda), which collectively nudge soundness down enough to prevent a higher overall score.
dhammabytes/S03E10_Sati_-_Knowing.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, philosophically rich talk with genuinely memorable framings—'knowing' as gerund, the butterfly image, the childhood memory of the Buddha—that move the listener toward practice, while the meditation guidance (stopping, returning to bare awareness) is practically sound and clearly sequenced, though the conceptual transitions between sati, paññā, vipassanā, and 'Buddha nature' are occasionally loose and could leave a practitioner uncertain how the pieces connect.

dhammabytes/S03E11_Sati_in_Daily_Life.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E11_Sati_in_Daily_Life.title: Sati in Daily Life
dhammabytes/S03E11_Sati_in_Daily_Life.full_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma delivers a warm, practically grounded talk with doctrinally sound guidance on sati, intention, and equanimity in daily life, drawing correctly on the Eightfold Path and the three unwholesome roots, while the prose is clear and occasionally illuminating (the gardener, the self-awareness paradox) though rarely transcendent, and the claim that absorbed action 'is the enlightened mind' is a slight overreach that mildly dents both soundness and inspiration.
dhammabytes/S03E11_Sati_in_Daily_Life.craft_reason: Bhante Bodhidhamma offers a warm, practically grounded talk with memorable framings—the gardener, the fencing conversation, the 'holiday' of non-becoming—and clear, well-sequenced guidance on attention, intention, and equanimity that a practitioner could genuinely act on, though the inspiration is pleasant rather than stirring and the conceptual distinctions (self-awareness vs. absorption, equanimity as 'default mode') are introduced but not fully developed.

dhammabytes/S03E12_Sila_-_Good_Conduct.speaker: Bhante Bodhidhamma
dhammabytes/S03E12_Sila_-_Good_Conduct.title: Sila - Good Conduct
